case_studies.title: Closing the Gap: Automated Discovery of Secure Dockerfile Reference Standards via Semantic Clustering in Enterprise Inner Source
case_studies.abstract: Containerization dominates enterprise software delivery, yet Dockerfiles that assemble container images frequently harbor security misconfigurations and structural technical debt. This problem is poorly understood in corporate inner-source environments, where proprietary context and isolated governance prevent direct application of open-source findings. We present an automated, six-stage pipeline that: (1) crawls an enterprise GitLab instance, (2) enriches each Dockerfile with static security and quality metrics (Hadolint, ShellCheck, Trivy) and lifecycle data, (3) groups functionally identical workloads using LLM-generated semantic descriptions and HDBSCAN, and (4) quantifies the optimization gap against cluster-internal reference implementations. Applied to 11,470 Dockerfiles from over 6,200 repositories at a single large industrial company, we find a systemic deficit: 99\% of files contain at least one security misconfiguration, 80.8\% violate Dockerfile best practices, and the median artifact has not been revised for 838~days. Despite this, high-quality reference implementations already exist within 83\% of functional clusters. Adopting these internal standards would increase the average security posture score by 60.4\% without developing any new templates. These findings, grounded in one organization's inner-source ecosystem, provide a data-driven foundation for future automated, context-aware recommender systems targeting enterprise supply-chain security; whether the observed technical-debt distribution and optimization gap generalize to other enterprises remains an open question for future multi-organization study.
case_studies.summary: The study builds a six‑step automated pipeline that crawls a corporate GitLab, enriches Dockerfiles with security and quality checks, clusters them using LLM‑generated semantics, and measures how far each file is from the best internal example. They found almost all Dockerfiles in a large company are insecure or outdated, but most clusters already contain a high‑quality reference, so switching to those could raise security scores by about 60%.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage container images, step 1: run the pipeline to collect and score all Dockerfiles in your GitLab. Step 2: use the cluster results to replace or refactor each file against the best‑performing reference in its cluster. Step 3: monitor security posture gains and maintain a rolling review cycle to keep the score above 60% improvement.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a concrete, operational pipeline that automates discovery of secure Dockerfile standards within an enterprise inner‑source environment, directly addressing a common infrastructure pain point for IT engineers. The method leverages existing tools (Hadolint, Trivy, ShellCheck) and LLMs for semantic clustering, indicating a mature, deployable solution rather than a purely theoretical proposal. The approach can be packaged and sold as a service to other organisations looking to improve container security, making monetisation highly actionable within 90 days.

case_studies.title: A Multi-Agent Platform for Automated Enterprise Analytics and Insight Generation
case_studies.abstract: This paper proposes a multi-agent framework built on CrewAI [1] for conversational business intelligence. Five specialized AI agents operate in a sequential pipeline to process natural language queries, retrieve and analyze data, generate visualizations via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) [2], and deliver actionable insights. The platform features a defense-in-depth security architecture for multi-tenant data isolation and a query parameterization mechanism for transforming conversational insights into reusable dashboard components. Evaluation across 300 end-to-end test cases spanning synthetic and production enterprise datasets demonstrates 95.3% functional accuracy, a mean response latency of 24 seconds, and a response quality score of 4.52/5.0 as assessed by an LLM-as-a-Judge framework, with a 93.0% hallucination-free rate, representing a 22.6 percentage point accuracy improvement and 20.2% quality gain over a single-agent baseline. Cross-model evaluation across four LLM backends and human expert validation confirm architectural generalizability and evaluator reliability. An ablation study confirms that the Data Analysis and Report Aggregation agents are the primary drivers of output quality.
case_studies.summary: The research delivers a multi‑agent system that turns natural language questions into business‑intelligence insights, using five specialised AI agents to pull, analyse, visualise and summarise data. They built a pipeline on CrewAI with a secure multi‑tenant design and a query‑parameterisation feature that turns conversations into reusable dashboards. The result was a 95.3% accuracy and 4.52/5 quality score with 93% of outputs free of hallucinations, outperforming single‑agent setups.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, check whether your data pipelines can plug into the platform’s secure multi‑tenant architecture: 1) ensure data isolation rules align with your compliance needs, 2) test the query‑parameterisation API against your existing dashboards, 3) monitor the 24‑second latency to confirm it meets your SLAs.
case_studies.relevance_tag: Enterprise Analytics, Multi-Agent Systems, BI Automation
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a practical multi-agent architecture that can be integrated into existing BI workflows, directly affecting IT engineers' work on enterprise analytics. The system is demonstrably built, evaluated, and ready for deployment, though it remains a research prototype. It offers actionable components that could be monetised as a SaaS or internal tooling within 90 days.

case_studies.title: Frustratingly Easy Agentic RAG via Portable Skills: A Case Study in Customer Support
case_studies.abstract: Enterprise workflow automation typically requires retrieving a complete and accurate set of relevant information from large operational document corpora (SOPs, policy documents) given a specific scenario or request. In customer support (CS), for example, human specialists must determine the correct sequence of resolution steps for each case, a task that demands precise grounding in policy documentation. Meeting this bar in production typically requires complex document chunking, indexing, and retrieval pipelines, often layered with learned re-rankers, query rewriters, and bespoke agentic RAG infrastructure. We report a deployment case study of a simpler alternative: a portable skill consisting of a natural-language instruction, lightweight tools (a retrieval API, format-checking scripts), and a corpus enriched with an LLM-generated navigation layer, which is a structured "Wikipedia-style" index over the underlying documents. This agentic RAG approach is straightforward to implement (1-2 engineer days), portable across capable agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code), and performs strongly on the challenging task of CS resolution workflow generation, achieving 99.2% procedural equivalence to human-approved ground truth and 83.3% evidence sufficiency. It is also roughly an order of magnitude slower per case than our deployed production assistant (~90 s vs. ~8-9 s), so we claim no latency advantage. Our claim is scoped to that setting: a mature, well-curated corpus, a latency-tolerant workflow, and human review of every case. There, the skill did the work of a complex RAG stack, and maintenance became a matter of editing text and data rather than retraining models.
case_studies.summary: The research tackles the difficulty of retrieving accurate policy information for customer support tasks. It builds a lightweight ‘portable skill’ that combines a natural‑language instruction, a simple retrieval API, and a LLM‑generated navigation layer acting as a structured index. The skill matches human‑approved procedures 99.2% of the time and provides sufficient evidence 83.3% of the time, replacing complex RAG stacks with a setup that takes only 1‑2 engineer days.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that hosts customer support bots, adopt the portable skill by: 1) creating a structured index of your SOPs using an LLM, 2) exposing a retrieval API to your agent, 3) adding lightweight format‑checking scripts; then test the skill’s procedural accuracy and evidence sufficiency before full deployment.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a deployable agentic RAG skill that simplifies customer support workflows, directly impacting IT engineering work with a low setup effort and high automation. The solution is already implemented and tested in production, demonstrating practical usability. IT engineers could adopt this skill or offer it as a service within a few days, making it commercially valuable.

case_studies.title: Statistical Detection of Positional Bias in LLM-Based Recommender Systems: Methodologies and Empirical Evidence
case_studies.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as recommendation generators in conversational recommender systems (RS) via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). This flexible design introduces new sources of structural bias. This paper studies positional bias in top-1 and single-turn LLM-based RS: systematic dependence of the recommended item on the order in which candidates are presented in the prompt. We propose two complementary detection methodologies: (i) POB-ICM, based on contingency matrix analysis and Chi-square independence testing, and (ii) POB-UNBP, a sample-efficient approach derived from a uniformity null model under permutation-based evaluation, enabling stochastic decoding with formal statistical guarantees. Using a controlled RAG testbed for product recommendation, built on a real product catalog, a fixed prompt template and 2000 template-generated user queries with 20 permutations each (40,000 instances), both methodologies reject the null hypothesis of positional independence and uniformity in all evaluated state-of-the-art models. We introduce three complementary metrics -- permutation sensitivity, positional bias, and strong positional bias -- to quantify this effect, the latter targeting cases where the position displaces the recommendation towards clearly less relevant items rather than only choosing among comparably relevant ones. A robustness analysis across candidate-set size and decoding temperature shows that the bias is structural and model-dependent, not an artifact of deterministic decoding or candidate-set size. These results establish positional bias as a measurable, reproducible property of prompt-mediated recommendation pipelines in the evaluated setting and motivate routine auditing and governance controls (e.g., order randomization, standardized prompting) for deployed LLM-based RS. Source code is publicly released.
case_studies.summary: The study shows that LLM‑based recommender systems can give different top‑1 items just because the order of candidates in the prompt changes – a clear positional bias. The authors built two statistical tests (POB‑ICM and POB‑UNBP) and applied them to a large RAG testbed, finding strong bias across all current models. This means your cloud‑hosted recommendation pipelines could be unfair or unreliable if you rely on LLM prompts, and you should audit them for order effects.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM‑based recommendation pipelines, first run the POB‑ICM or POB‑UNBP tests on your prompts; second, randomise the order of candidate items or standardise prompt templates to minimise bias; third, monitor bias metrics (permutation sensitivity, positional bias) as part of your routine quality checks.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces practical detection methods for positional bias in LLM-powered recommender systems, with publicly available code and a testbed, making it directly usable for IT engineers who deploy or maintain such systems. The methods are mature and can be turned into a service or integrated tool within 90 days. While the impact on core infrastructure is moderate, it is still relevant for engineers managing recommendation pipelines.

case_studies.title: AI Assisted Workflow Optimization and Automation
case_studies.abstract: Against the backdrop of digital transformation and stricter regulation, enterprise compliance work demands higher efficiency and accuracy. The auxiliary compliance process has become an important entry point for optimizing the compliance system due to its strong transactional nature and high degree of repetition. This study focuses on the process characteristics of auxiliary compliance work, sorts out its structural composition and organizational mechanism, proposes an optimization path with process reengineering, system modeling, and technology integration as the core, and focuses on exploring the collaborative application of key technologies such as RPA, rule engine, and semantic recognition in process automation. Research suggests that the systematic optimization and intelligent upgrading of auxiliary processes will help build a modern compliance operation system that is responsive, efficient, structurally clear, and risk controllable.
case_studies.summary: The study tackles the inefficiency of repetitive compliance tasks by building an integrated automation framework that uses RPA, rule engines, and semantic recognition to re‑engineer and model auxiliary compliance processes. The result is a modern, risk‑controlled compliance system that is faster, clearer and more responsive.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, check if your compliance workflows use manual or legacy tools; replace them with the described RPA + rule‑engine stack, then monitor for reduced cycle time and error rates.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes an integration of RPA, rule engines, and semantic recognition for compliance workflow automation, directly relevant to IT infrastructure and enterprise SaaS tools. It appears to be a proposal with some implementation hints but not a fully deployed system, hence moderate maturity. The concepts are actionable enough that an IT engineer could implement or sell them as a compliance automation service within a short timeframe. Overall impact and monetisation are solid, leading to a strong total score.
